title: Did Archibald James marry Elizabeth Breakey, and was little Archie their son?
desc: The narrator's central puzzle. The diary and Eliza Nelson's letters imply a marriage, but "there is no record of that marriage" {q:168-170}; that Archie was the son of Archibald and Elizabeth is "believed, but not conclusively proven" {q:108, 130}. The narrator connects it to the dormant baronetcy {q:174}.
alternatives: Married (perhaps irregularly or abroad) and Archie legitimate
Not married; Archie illegitimate but acknowledged by his grandparents
Archie the son of Archibald by another woman
next: Search Church of Ireland and Presbyterian registers for Ballybay/Monaghan 1822–24 and Barbados/Trinidad marriage registers; re-read the diary and Nelson letters; trace Archie's later life.

title: Who was the eighth son of Captain William and Eliza?
desc: Ten children, "eight boys and two girls" {q:84, 96}, but only seven sons are named: William Henry, Archibald James, John Churchill, Corry, Tenison Alan, Bellingham and Samuel. When the narrator lost the name of the brother after Archibald {q:112-114}, the interviewer supplied John Churchill from Crisp's {q:126}.
alternatives: Named in the Crisp's entry but not read out
The count of eight is a slip
next: Read the full Crisp's (Visitation of Ireland) pedigree.

title: Tenison or Tennyson?
desc: The transcript writes "Tennyson" throughout {q:14, 102}. Eliza Bellingham's mother was Elizabeth Tenison and her brother Henry Tenison Bellingham {s:lf-bellingham}, so Tenison is very probably the true spelling, and "Alan" echoes her brother Alan.
next: Confirm from Constabulary records or his marriage entry.

title: When, and through whom, did Tenison get his Constabulary appointment?
desc: Tenison returned in 1840 {q:204}; the narrator credits Sir William Somerville as Chief Secretary {q:212-214}, but Sir William held that office only from July 1847 {s:wp-1st-baron}. Either the appointment came later than the return, or it was obtained through Sir William's influence as an MP (from 1837) or Home Office minister (1846–47).
next: RIC/Irish Constabulary officer registers (National Archives UK, HO 184) for Tenison's date of appointment.

title: The other children of Tenison and Eliza O'Connor
desc: Only Bellingham Arthur and an unnamed elder brother (also RIC) are mentioned {q:12}. The narrator moves straight from Tenison's household to Bellingham Arthur's children, listing "again a number of children" who are his uncles and aunts {q:216-218}. We read that list as Bellingham Arthur's family, because it ends with "my father, Reginald".
next: Dublin civil and church registers (from 1845/1864) for children of Tenison Somerville.

title: Is the 1887 "District Inspector Somerville" Bellingham Arthur?
desc: Hansard and local histories name only "District Inspector Somerville" {s:hansard-1887} {s:ballymacoda-1887}. The family story (RIC detachment from Cork to Youghal, a rioter named Hanlon killed with a blade, arrest, Parliament, no conviction) matches closely {q:312-322}. The narrator remembered the 1880s and "Captain" Somerville, and a fishing dispute.
next: Cork Examiner / Freeman's Journal reports of the March 1887 inquest; RIC registers for D.I. Somerville's full name and stations.

title: Captain William's regiments
desc: Family tradition: South Cork Light Infantry, "allegedly"; perhaps North Cork; "searches have been made in the military records" without success {q:54-56}. Later a militia officer ("the Laos … country … militia") {q:56}. We read this as the Louth Militia, his father-in-law's regiment {s:lf-bellingham}; Laois is the alternative.
alternatives: A regular regiment, later the Louth or Queen's County (Laois) Militia
next: Militia officer lists in the Army Lists c. 1795–1830.

title: Captain William: born 1776 or 1777?
desc: Narrator: 1777, "I think" {q:62}. Published Bellingham genealogy: 1776 {s:lf-bellingham}.

title: Who was "Sir William Somerville the younger" at Ardrass?
desc: "Sir William Somerville, the younger, inherited the house, Ardrass? … We don't know. I don't know. I suspect he did" {q:90}. It is unclear whether this is a question from the interviewer, a different branch, or a confusion with Captain William.
next: NLI Registered Pedigree of the Somervilles of Ardrass {s:nli-ardrass}.

title: Who sold Castle Bellingham to Sir William: Alan or his widow?
desc: Narrator: Alan "sold it, actually, to his uncle" {q:36}. Published genealogy: Alan rented it to Sir William, and Monique sold the freehold by c. 1824, after Alan's death in 1821 {s:lf-bellingham}. Both agree that it passed to the uncle.

title: The cousin in Canada who gave family members "a leg up"
desc: "There was a cousin … regiment … in Canada, and he appears in the records as … giving a leg up to a number of family members"; "one of the Bellinghams was a descendant of an early settler in Canada" {q:30-34}. The transcript is badly garbled here ("a regiment law for sale"). Monique's family, the Bâbys, were early French settlers of Detroit, which may be what is meant.

title: Was Dorothea or Eliza the eldest sister?
desc: Narrator: "Dorothea being Eliza's eldest sister" {q:144}. Published genealogy: Elizabeth b. 1779, Dorothea b. c. 1780, though Dorothea married first (1798) {s:lf-bellingham}.

title: Where did Archibald spend "a few days" before sailing?
desc: Diary as remembered: "spent a few days include Mal, and then took ship" {q:148}. Best reading: Clonmel, where his aunt Dorothea Riall lived {s:lf-bellingham}. The port of embarkation is not stated.

title: The house called "Farm"
desc: "Another house, called Farm, just called Farm … about Herbert, in County cotton" {q:182}. Probably near Belturbet, Co. Cavan.

title: Locate Cumry, Co. Monaghan
desc: Spelled out by the narrator as C-U-M-R-Y {q:136}, near Ballybay {q:162}. Not yet found in townland indexes.
next: Search townlands.ie and Griffith's Valuation for Ballybay parish.

title: "Livingston Avenue", Rathmines
desc: Tenison and Eliza's later home {q:216}. No such street has been confirmed; it may be a mishearing.

title: Bellingham Arthur's boyhood nickname
desc: "As a boy he was known as fighting atte … atte being Arthur" {q:24}. Possibly "Fighting Artie"; unclear.

title: First name of the daughter who married Edmund Truell
desc: Transcribed "there to money" {q:224}; the interviewer remarks that it is an unusual name.

title: Henry Rock: surname spelling
desc: "Henry Rock" / "Henry Oak" {q:232-234}. Possibly Rooke. A 1912 Dublin marriage would settle it.

title: Bunt's regiment: King's Own (Royal Lancaster) or Royal Artillery?
desc: Narrator: Royal Lancaster Regiment in WWI {q:364}. A war-diary-based history lists "Lt. Col. W A T B Somerville DSO (Royal Artillery)" commanding the 8th (Special) Bn MGC in 1919 {s:mgc-8bn}. He may have changed regiments, or the narrator may have transposed Bunt's and Jim's (Jim was Royal Artillery {q:366}).
next: Army Lists 1914–19; London Gazette DSO citation.

title: Pat's capture, camps and escape
desc: Captured in the retreat from Mons; escaped at the third attempt; MC {q:442-450}. The family has photographs from the camps {q:452}. Battalion, camps and escape date are unknown. A published MC record for a different escaped Royal Warwickshire officer (Gualter Somerville) must not be confused with him.
next: ICRC First World War prisoners archive; National Archives (UK) WO 339 officer file; London Gazette for the MC.

title: "Gunners Venture" in Kenya
desc: {q:498-500} No independent record found yet under that name.

title: "Green desert" between Bantry and Glengarriff
desc: Where Bunt and Kitty's cottages and gardens were {q:374, 554}. The name is surely misheard.

title: Where is Uncle Jim buried?
desc: "He's buried in Matthew" {q:388}. Unidentified; possibly Rathnew or another Wicklow churchyard.

title: When was Clermont sold?
desc: Narrator: settled "about 1950 … '52, '53" {q:566}. Heritage record: c. 1955; the religious order arrived in 1956 {s:wicklowheritage-clermont} {s:irishaesthete-clermont}.

title: Was Kitty Harrison previously married to Alan Ferguson?
desc: "She married. Or she hadn't married. An Australian … Alan Ferguson" {q:374}.

title: The Johnson ancestry
desc: Comes mainly from the interviewer's Ancestry tree, read aloud in a confused passage {q:520-524}: the Rector of Wicklow (possibly Philip), his father Samuel, and Samuel's father Zachariah (or Samuel the Elder), with a Frances Tench. All unverified.
next: Clergy of Dublin and Glendalough succession lists for the Rectors of Wicklow; Church of Ireland records.

title: "William P. … William J." in the online tree
desc: The interviewer reads out entries ("Henry, son of William J … William P, who is father of William J … William Padlu?") {q:118-120} that cannot be matched to anyone in the narrator's account.

title: Whose deaths prompted the destruction of the diary?
desc: "Following the death of my great-grandparents, my aunt Eddie's parents, the end of the 19th century" {q:134}. Eddie's parents died in 1916 and 1949; the narrator's great-grandparents (Tenison and Eliza, Eddie's grandparents) died before c. 1895 {q:216}. We read "parents" as a slip for "grandparents".

title: Date of the recording
desc: The file is labelled "27 Oct" with no year. Internal clues: the narrator, born 1937, is "coming up to 90" {q:50}, and it is half-term. This suggests 2026.

title: Where are the original papers?
desc: The recording refers to Bellingham Arthur's six volumes {q:6}, transcripts of Captain William's diary {q:132}, Eliza's letters {q:52}, the Nelson correspondence {q:166}, the Crisp's entry {q:124}, Bellingham Arthur's official and personal diaries {q:334}, portraits of Dorothea and Monique and a miniature of Henry {q:26-28, 36, 44}, Pat's camp photographs {q:452}, Reginald's Kenya photographs {q:504}, and Monique's booklet {q:42}. Cousin Eliza began photographing the portraits {q:46}. An inventory, with scans linked from this archive, is the most valuable next step.
